Refactor the guillotine rectangle DP into a function and run it on two grid resolutions, G=12 and then G=20 (about 1/5 and 1/10 steps). The G=20 pass runs only if time allows (deadline checks), and the best of all candidates is emitted.

I raised the guillotine rectangle DP's size limit from n≤90 to n≤250, so larger n also get the non-square strip constructions. Make the maximum grid size M in the recursive-grid DP adaptive. It rises from 8 to 12 for n up to about 300, so larger n can use k×k grids with k up to 12 directly. For very large n it is capped by a cost budget, which keeps the O(C·n²) loop within the time limit. I haven't run it.

Use a finer 24×24 integer grid for the guillotine rectangle DP when n ≤ 40, instead of 12×12. Every 12-grid cut is also a 24-grid cut, so this is a superset and can only match or beat the old result. It also allows cuts at 1/24 steps, and the extra time cost is a few seconds. I haven't run it.

I vectorised the O(C·n²) inner loop of the recursive-grid DP with numpy, using the same tie-breaking as before. The results should be unchanged, but large n should now finish well inside the time limit. I haven't run it.

Replaces the grid with a guillotine-partition dynamic program: for several integer resolutions G it computes the best sum of sides for m squares in every a×b integer rectangle, using all cuts and all splits of m, and then reconstructs the best layout. Search many more grid resolutions: every G from 1 to 30 plus a few finer ones up to 60, with the existing time-budget guard skipping any that won't fit. This lets the guillotine DP find layouts whose cut positions aren't multiples of the earlier coarse G values, for example thirds or sevenths.

After the guillotine DP builds its layout, I add an LP polish. It fixes each pair's separating axis and direction from the DP layout, then maximises the sum of sides over the continuous positions and sizes.
